summary.title: How to build a knowledge factory for AI agents
summary.idea: Agents fail at company work because tacit knowledge is scattered; a loop of agents flagging gaps and a background curator agent updating skills and docs keeps that knowledge current.
howItWorks: Split knowledge into three kinds: skills (how to do work), domain facts, and data-access guidance on where to query.
Give working agents a tool to report missing or wrong information, optionally suggesting the correct fix.
Run a background curator agent on a schedule with access to raw sources, agent traces, and flagged issues.
Let only the curator edit the knowledge, so working agents don't create contradictions.
Keep storage simple (skills in GitHub, a wiki page) since no standard format has emerged yet.
summary.stealThis: Before your next recurring agent workflow, add a 'flag_knowledge_issue' tool and a nightly curator job that reads flags and session traces, then updates the relevant skill files.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running agents on recurring business workflows and their skills or docs keep going stale or contradicting each other.
summary.quote: The goal isn’t to document everything before agents can start working.

verdict.reason: Teaches a portable knowledge-maintenance loop that doesn't need LangChain's product: working agents get a flag-issue tool, and a scheduled curator agent reads flags and traces to update skills; a worked revenue-report example shows it, though there's no code or repo.

summary.title: Check what your AI agents do before they do it, with Semantic governance policies
summary.idea: Agent permissions say what a tool can do, not whether a given call follows your rules, so an out-of-band LLM judge checks each proposed tool call against plain-language policies and the user's request.
howItWorks: A gateway intercepts the model's response and holds any proposed tool call before the agent can run it.
An LLM judge sees the conversation, system instructions, tool descriptions and your written policies, then allows or denies.
Each call must pass two checks: your plain-language rules and a built-in check that it matches what the user asked.
Denied calls are replaced with a custom message; every verdict and rationale is logged for audit.
Start in dry run mode, review logged verdicts, then switch to enforcement.
summary.stealThis: Before giving an agent a risky tool like email or delete, write one plain-language policy with explicit exceptions (such as 'regardless of NDAs or urgency') and have a separate judge check each proposed call in log-only mode first.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're putting agents with real side effects (email, deletes, payments) into production and want a check that injection or a persuasive user can't bypass.

verdict.reason: Despite being a Preview launch, it teaches a portable pre-execution gate you could rebuild as a tool-call hook: an out-of-band LLM judge checks each proposed call against plain-language policies (with explicit exceptions like NDAs) plus a user-intent check, logs its verdicts, and runs in dry run before enforcement; it is thin because the only code configures Google's product.

summary.title: mattpocock/skills: Skills for Real Engineers
summary.idea: Agents misunderstand intent, ramble, ship broken code and bloat the design; a set of small, composable skills targets each failure with grilling sessions, a shared glossary, TDD loops and design reviews.
howItWorks: Run /grill-me or /grill-with-docs so the agent interviews you about the plan before any code is written.
Grilling builds a glossary and ADRs, giving the agent short shared terms instead of long descriptions.
The /tdd skill enforces red-green-refactor, and /diagnosing-bugs builds a failing feedback loop before attempting any fix.
The /code-review skill runs Standards and Spec reviews as parallel sub-agents so neither pollutes the other.
Skills are either user-invoked orchestrators or model-invoked disciplines; user-invoked ones never call other user-invoked ones.
summary.stealThis: Before your next feature, have the agent grill you with one question at a time until every branch is settled, and save new jargon in a GLOSSARY.md.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building your own skills library and want a tested, adaptable set of small skills covering planning, testing, review and design.
summary.quote: The rate of feedback is your speed limit.

verdict.reason: A working, MIT-licensed skills library: grilling sessions before coding, a GLOSSARY.md shared language, TDD and gated bug-diagnosis loops, and two-axis parallel sub-agent code review, each with its rationale and the actual skill files to copy.

summary.title: I Moved my Claude Code Workflow Scripts Into Skills Any Agent Harness Can Run
summary.idea: Workflow scripts tied to one vendor can't ask the human mid-run; packaging the procedure as an Agent Skill with a small Python referee keeps code-controlled steps but works in any harness.
howItWorks: A skill holds SKILL.md, a flow.py defining steps and order, and one prompt file per step.
The main session runs flow.py, which prints the next launch; the session starts a subagent with that exact text.
Each subagent returns typed JSON, such as findings count, and flow.py's code decides whether to fix, ask the human, or end.
Steps hand work over through files in a run directory, and state.json lets a fresh session resume the run.
Each step names an executor model, so a Codex reviewer can follow a Claude coder without relay hacks.
summary.stealThis: Before your next multi-step agent task, write the order and loop limit as a small flow script that prints the next step, and have the session obey it, pausing to ask you when the fix budget runs out.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running multi-agent coding procedures with review loops and want vendor-neutral orchestration that can pause for human decisions and survive lost sessions.
summary.quote: The model does the step. The code picks the next step.

verdict.reason: A real working harness with code, an open-source repo, a worked run and stats from 300+ runs: a Python 'referee' flow script that prints the next subagent launch, typed JSON replies, file-based state for resuming and human-ask on budget exhaustion — all portable across harnesses.

summary.title: AI agents open 17 million pull requests a month. I built a gate that rejects the ones that lie.
summary.idea: Agent PRs that say 'fixed' are only claims, so a deterministic Python gate checks the actual commit for tampered tests, deleted functions, regressions and vacuous new tests before any human reviews.
howItWorks: Tamper scan flags existing tests that were edited, deleted or weakened to make the build pass.
Public API check fails the PR if a function the project had is now gone.
A new test only counts if it fails on the old code and passes on the new.
A hidden suite the agent never sees must also confirm the bug is gone.
Gate findings are fed back to the agent, which proposes three candidate fixes per round and keeps the best.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent-driven bug fix merges, require a test that fails on the old commit and passes on the new one, and reject any diff that touches existing assertions.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're reviewing agent PRs by hand and want a concrete, open-source merge gate, plus a comment thread debating hidden-suite blind spots and mutation testing.

verdict.reason: Teaches a portable deterministic merge gate for agent PRs: a tamper scan on existing tests, a public-API check, fail-on-old/pass-on-new for new tests, and a hidden suite. It backs these with an open-source repo, real run numbers and failure stories. The comments add concrete mutation-testing code; Kiro and Nova are incidental to the technique.

summary.title: Our agent reviews its own mistakes every day. Here is the loop, and the tests it produced
summary.idea: An agent repeats the same routine mistakes, so a daily self-review built from counted metrics turns repeated causes into queued code fixes, each backed by a test, rather than relying on the agent remembering lessons.
howItWorks: The platform starts the review itself once per day, instead of a cron task typed into a pane that got lost.
The prompt uses counted figures: failed turns, tool errors, owner corrections, and decisions the owner said the agent could have made.
Tool calls are split into real mistakes and calls a safety gate blocked on purpose, so working guardrails aren't flagged as bugs.
The agent updates a lessons note, saves a daily memory entry, and appends one queue line per repeated cause with the code fix wanted.
Fixes land in separate upgrade rounds, each with a test named after the review or queue item that found it.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent tuning session, log tool failures and gate refusals separately, then have the agent write one 'cause; evidence; fix' queue line per repeated failure, and turn each into a test.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running agents for long stretches and want a concrete pattern for turning repeated tool errors into code changes and tests.
summary.quote: A bare "failed" gives a model nothing to do except try the same thing again.

verdict.reason: A real, open-source setup showing a daily self-review loop built from counted metrics, with tool errors split from gate refusals, a queue line format turning repeated causes into code fixes with named tests, and the portable lesson of rewriting error messages to carry the next step; it is vendor-built but replicable without the product, with concrete examples and not much code inline.

summary.title: A checklist for reviewing a pull request an AI agent wrote
summary.idea: Agent PRs look tidy and confident but come without the context you have for a colleague's work, so review should target the places agents typically cut corners, in a fixed order.
howItWorks: Write a one-sentence statement of what the PR should do before reading code, and use it as the yardstick.
Check diff stats and treat the PR description as a claim to verify, not a summary.
Read changed tests first, looking for weakened assertions, deleted cases, skipped tests or updated expected values.
Scrutinise dependencies, swallowed errors, CI or lint config, auth and secrets, outbound calls, and string-built shell or SQL.
Automate the rest: lockfile-without-manifest CI failures, code owners on sensitive files, linting for skipped tests and swallowed exceptions.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent PR review, write one sentence of what it should do, then open the changed tests first and look for loosened assertions or skipped cases.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're reviewing agent-written PRs regularly and want a ready-made, risk-ordered checklist plus ideas for automating its checks.
summary.quote: Treat it as a claim to verify, not a summary to trust.

verdict.reason: A concrete, risk-ordered checklist for agent PRs (one-sentence yardstick, read changed tests first for weakened assertions, scrutinise deps/config/auth) plus automation ideas like lockfile-without-manifest CI failures and code owners, but with no code, examples or before/after evidence it is a thin, near-generic checklist.

summary.title: How Non-Engineers Now Assign Work to Coding Agents
summary.idea: Non-engineers can't safely run coding agents in a terminal, so put the agent on a shared task board where a plain-language task becomes a pull request that an engineer reviews before merge.
howItWorks: An engineer sets up agents once, with repo access, credentials and a GitHub link, so they appear as assignees.
Non-engineers file tasks from the board, Slack or Jira, with an optional triage step to check size first.
Each agent works in its own isolated worktree, so several tasks run in parallel without clashing.
The PR carries the task ID, links back to the task, and an engineer reviews it before merging.
Start with low-risk work such as copy, translations and small UI fixes, and keep production, auth and payments with engineers.
summary.stealThis: Before handing a small fix to an agent, write the task with five parts (what's wrong, what done looks like, where, a screenshot, and what not to touch), and treat a missing 'done' as a sign to ask an engineer first.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're an engineer or PM looking to let non-engineers hand small tasks to coding agents without losing review control.
summary.quote: The non-engineer starts the work, the agent does the first draft, and an engineer decides what ships.

verdict.reason: Despite the Sharkly pitch, the post teaches portable techniques: a five-part task template with a before/after example, a 'can't write done means not ready' rule, a risk-tiered handoff table and PR-only guardrails, though it is fairly basic.

summary.title: Loop discipline in hooks, and the skill rewrite
summary.idea: Loop rules written as prose get skipped, so this setup moves them into Claude Code hooks that inject context at session start, block premature stopping, and relay a stop file, plus a slimmer skill.
howItWorks: SessionStart hook injects a size-capped context: preflight verdict, selected work, vision goals, recent learnings and latest metrics.
Stop hook blocks ending once while state shows a cycle begun but not ended, and allows it when stop_hook_active is set.
PostToolUse hook checks for a .loop/STOP file and tells the agent to finish or park, clean up and end.
The PreToolUse guard refuses edits to the hook scripts, so the agent cannot loosen its own rules.
Hook tests run under dash, validate the settings shape with jq, and a headless claude -p smoke test confirms each hook fires.
summary.stealThis: Before your next long-running agent loop, add a Stop hook that blocks once while a cycle-open flag is set, and honor stop_hook_active so it cannot trap the session.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building an unattended agent loop and want a worked example of hooks, a size-capped context injection and a hook test script.
summary.quote: Move the loop's rules out of prose and into hooks

verdict.reason: A real working harness that moves loop rules from prose into Claude Code hooks: size-capped SessionStart context, a Stop hook that blocks once and honours stop_hook_active, a STOP-file relay, a guard against editing hooks, and hook tests plus a headless smoke test, though no actual code is shown and much of the context is project-specific.

summary.title: chight1/pr-verify: A CI gate for pull requests, then a Claude review whose findings are each proven by a test the harness runs
summary.idea: Agent code reviews post plausible but unproven claims; this pipeline runs a deterministic CI gate first, then lets a Claude reviewer post only findings backed by a test the harness shows failing.
howItWorks: A model-free CI gate (lint, types, build, tests, audit, scans) is the only thing that can block a merge.
The review agent gets four tools only: read_file, run_tests, propose_patch, finish. It has no shell, network or search.
On finish, the harness replays each claim from a clean checkout: a bug is verified if the test patch alone fails the suite.
A fix is verified only if the test and fix patches together make the suite pass; unproven claims are labelled unverified and capped at three.
Each run writes a JSON record with tool-call trail, token use and verification results, and budgets for tokens, calls and time stop runaway runs.
summary.stealThis: Make your review agent attach a failing test to every behavioral claim, and have a script (not the agent) re-run that test on a clean checkout before the comment is posted.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building a review agent or CI gate and want enforced guardrails, sandboxing and budgets rather than prompt requests.
summary.quote: The review is advisory. A person decides what to do with it.

verdict.reason: A working, MIT-licensed repo teaches a portable technique: every review-agent claim must come with a failing test that the harness, not the agent, replays from a clean checkout, backed by a restricted toolset, caps on unverified findings, budgets and a JSON run record, all matching the card.

summary.title: Limit pull request reviews to one round sized to the diff
summary.idea: Agent review loops that run until nothing new turns up never end, because a reviewer can always find a word to change; the fix is one review round sized to the diff.
howItWorks: Give each pull request one review round, with depth scaled to the size and risk of the diff.
Add a second check, such as a skeptic trying to refute a finding, only when it changes a decision, claim or code.
Apply wording fixes directly, with no further review round.
If an owner answer changes the diff afterward, review only the changed lines once more.
Make the rule hold at every effort level, including the max-effort mode.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent-run batch of pull requests, write a review-budget rule (one round, sized to the diff, skeptic checks only for substantive findings) and compare cost per PR against a looped run.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running agent review loops and watching costs climb, or you want a real example of turning cost data into a written harness rule.
summary.quote: A review that loops until it finds nothing new does not end on prose, because a reviewer can always find a word to change.

verdict.reason: A real harness rule backed by session cost data: about $11–20 per PR versus about $85 for looped review. The technique is one review round sized to the diff, skeptic checks only for findings that change a decision, claim or code, wording fixes applied without re-review, and a re-review of only the changed lines when an owner answer changes the diff. It is narrow but directly copyable, and the card matches the page.
